title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 26 Aug 2026]
    Title:Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

report.summary: Harness configuration, not just model weights, substantially changes coding-agent performance; evaluations must treat model-plus-harness as the tested solver.
report.background: Coding agents are typically viewed as a single AI model, but in practice they are systems: the model is wrapped in a harness that controls context, tools, and workflow. This paper systematically tests whether that harness matters by keeping the same model and benchmark tasks fixed while changing only how the harness manages conversation history and tool outputs. The control preserves the full conversation; the treatment truncates old tool results under context pressure and reacts to repeated or stalled work. Results show large performance gaps, especially under tight context windows, where the treatment improved fail-to-pass rates and complete solutions. The authors argue this undermines common evaluations that credit model weights alone, since the same frozen weights can produce very different outcomes depending on incremental harness decisions. This has direct implications for coding-agent research, benchmarking standards, and product comparisons.
key_points: The harness is a decisive variable: with the same model and fixed tasks, changing only how tool outputs are shortened and how stalled work is handled changed results. This shows a coding agent is best understood as a model-plus-harness system, not just a model, and that baseline comparisons need to control for harness choices.

Under tight context constraints on SWE-bench Verified, the treatment raised mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction from 28 percent to 49 percent and increased complete solutions from 43 to 72 across 169 tasks. The same pattern held across all three pressure comparisons, demonstrating meaningful gains when context is scarce.

The frozen treatment also improved outcomes for three additional models without retuning, suggesting the context-management strategy generalizes across model architectures. That means harness-level fixes can unlock capability without waiting for larger or better models, and they may compound with future model improvements.

In wide-context comparisons, gains were smaller but still visible: FeatureBench retained a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment, and on wide-window Verified the treatment consumed fewer prompt tokens per turn. This implies harness efficiency and performance benefits persist even when context is plentiful, potentially lowering cost and latency.

Evaluation practice must change: comparing models without specifying harness details can rank them misleadingly. Since the same weights can look weak or strong depending on the harness, benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro should report both components together and standardize harness configurations for apples-to-apples comparisons.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this study shifts part of the coding-agent roadmap from model scaling to harness engineering. Model providers can no longer claim benchmark results solely on weights, while startup teams may find that better memory and tool-output management can rival or amplify model upgrades. Developers building agentic coding tools should expect open-source harnesses to become a core differentiator, with context-window policies becoming a first-class performance lever. For regular users, it means product-level coding-agent quality depends heavily on implementation details rather than the advertised model, and practical gains like faster token usage and fewer stalled tasks can come from harness improvements. Benchmarking bodies and evaluation papers should adopt a model-plus-harness framing, or public leaderboards will keep obscuring the true source of progress.
report.tools: To explore these ideas hands-on, watch SWE-agent and OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin), both open-source harnesses for agentic software engineering, and Aider for LLM pair-programming. For benchmarks, SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro are the key evaluation suites; FeatureBench adds another stress test. Readers may also follow terminal-bench and Moatless Tools for context-sensitive agent workflows.
